sanguine

/SANG-gwin/ - rhymes with penguin · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sanguine means optimistic, cheery.

Down three games to one, the manager stayed oddly sanguine, penciling in the same lineup and predicting a comeback by Sunday.

Example

The startup's servers crashed on launch morning, but its founder stayed sanguine on the all-hands call: 'We patch tonight, we relaunch Friday, and in a year this is the story we tell at parties.'

Sanguine is optimism as a temperament — confident good cheer that holds up in bad weather. Hopeful people want the good outcome; sanguine people expect it. Medieval doctors thought the mood came from a healthy supply of blood, and the word still carries that ruddy, unbothered glow.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hopeful: Hopeful means wanting and wishing for the good outcome — hope reaches for good news but stops short of forecasting it. Sanguine goes further and expects: cheerful, settled confidence that things will come right. Hope crosses its fingers; sanguine checks the calendar and smiles.

confident: Confident means sure of the outcome — certainty, with or without a smile. Sanguine adds the good cheer and makes the whole outlook a temperament: a sanguine person meets bad news still cheerfully expecting things to come right. You can be grimly confident; nobody is grimly sanguine.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

gloomy: expecting the worst, and glum about it

pessimistic: convinced the bad outcome is the likely one

Where it sits · how little doubt is left

wishful → sanguine → blithe

wishful vs. sanguine: Wishful is wanting without expecting — milder than sanguine, which genuinely believes the good news is coming.

blithe vs. sanguine: Blithe goes further than sanguine — the sanguine planner expects things to work out and still checks the forecast; the blithe one has stopped checking anything at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sangu: blood (Latin sanguis)

Suffix — -ine: adjective ending: of, like (as in marine, canine)

Put it together: Sangu- (blood) + -ine (of, like) = of the blood. Medieval medicine taught that four bodily fluids set your temperament, and the lucky people governed by blood were ruddy-cheeked, warm, and cheerfully confident — sanguine. The science is long dead; the personality label refuses to die.

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin sanguis, 'blood,' built almost nothing else you'd meet in an ordinary English day — its other descendants (sanguinary, consanguinity) are rare legal and literary visitors. Learn sanguine on its own, and let the four-humors story hold it in memory.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Sanguine is the polished word for durable optimism — analysts are sanguine about earnings, captains stay sanguine in storms. It is steadier than upbeat (in this unit's reference list) and roomier than hopeful: hope wants, sanguine expects. In this unit's weather system, sanguine is the climate while elated is a single sunny burst.
